lessons.title: Tree Basics
lessons.concept: A tree is a non-linear, hierarchical data structure with nodes connected by edges. Binary tree: each node has at most 2 children. BST: left < root < right.
lessons.formula: BST: left subtree < node < right subtree
lessons.worked_example: BST Inorder traversal (Left → Root → Right) visits nodes in ascending order.

lessons.title: Tree Traversal
lessons.worked_example: BST Inorder visits nodes in non-decreasing (ascending) order.

practice.question: Which is not a linear data structure?
practice.explanation: Tree is non-linear (hierarchical). Others are linear.

practice.question: BST Inorder traversal visits nodes in?
practice.explanation: Inorder (Left → Root → Right) of a BST visits in ascending order.

practice.question: The topmost node of a tree is called the:
practice.explanation: The root is the ancestor of all nodes (the entry point of the tree); leaves are nodes with no children.

practice.question: A node with no children is called a:
practice.explanation: Leaves (external nodes) have no children; internal nodes have at least one child.
practice.provenance: Authored for BountyCode as original practice/question item; not scraped from third-party sources. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

practice.question: A binary tree node contains at most how many children?
practice.explanation: Binary = two: each node has at most a left and a right child.
practice.provenance: Authored for BountyCode as original practice/question item; not scraped from third-party sources. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

practice.question: The depth (height) of a single-node tree is:
practice.explanation: With edges counting levels, a lone root has height 0 (some texts use 1 node-count convention; edge convention gives 0).

practice.question: Pre-order traversal visits nodes in which order?
practice.explanation: Pre-order = Root first, then subtrees (Left, Right). In-order = Left, Root, Right; post-order = Left, Right, Root.
practice.provenance: Authored for BountyCode as original practice/question item; not scraped from third-party sources. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

questions.question: Graph BFS/DFS time complexity?
questions.explanation: BFS/DFS visit each vertex once and each edge once → O(V+E).

questions.question: Level-order traversal of a binary tree uses which structure?
questions.explanation: Level-order (BFS) processes nodes left-to-right level by level: enqueue the root, then enqueue children of each dequeued node.

questions.question: How many nodes does a FULL binary tree of height h have (root at height 0)?
questions.explanation: A full tree of height h (levels 0..h) has 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^h = 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes. If h is defined as the number of levels, the formula is 2^h - 1; with root height 0 it is 2^(h+1) - 1.

questions.question: In-order traversal of a binary SEARCH tree yields elements in:
questions.explanation: In-order (left, root, right) visits smaller keys before the root and larger after, producing sorted ascending output - the standard BST property check.
questions.provenance: Authored for BountyCode as original practice/question item; not scraped from third-party sources. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

questions.question: The maximum number of nodes at level k of a binary tree is:
questions.explanation: Level k (root = level 0) can hold up to 2^k nodes since each level doubles the branching capacity.
questions.provenance: Authored for BountyCode as original practice/question item; not scraped from third-party sources. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

questions.question: Post-order traversal of a binary tree is useful for:

options.A: Printing a directory listing with sub-folder sizes (process children first)

questions.explanation: Post-order processes children before the parent - exactly what recursive deletion, expression evaluation (operands then operator) and subtree aggregation need.

questions.question: In a binary SEARCH tree, for every node all keys in the left subtree are:
questions.explanation: BST invariant: left subtree keys < node key < right subtree keys (with a consistent duplicate policy), which is what makes search O(h).

questions.question: Searching a balanced BST of n nodes takes:
questions.explanation: Each comparison descends one level; a balanced tree has O(log n) height, giving O(log n) search (degenerating to O(n) when skewed).
